extracted.intended_audience: researchers and statisticians assessing inter-rater reliability (two raters), clinicians and authors who use Kappa statistics in studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, computing, interpreting, and reporting Kappa-family inter-rater reliability statistics when there are precisely two raters (including when to use Cohen's Kappa vs weighted Kappa and what to report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen’s Kappa suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen’s Kappa is a frequently employed classical statistical method to assess IRR, and it’s only suitable for fully-crossed designs with precisely two raters. Cohen’s Kappa is commonly used for two raters with two categories or for unordered categorical variables with three or more categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes formula for Cohen’s Kappa. Advantages: accounts for chance agreement and is applicable to categorical variables with two or more categories. Limitations/anti-patterns: sensitive to prevalence of categories (can be biased when categories are imbalanced) and assumes rater independence — violations can lead to inaccurate estimates. When data are ordered (ordinal) with three or more categories, consider alternatives (weighted Kappa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted Kappa suitability (LWK and QWK)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a need to evaluate agreement between two raters regarding ordered categorical variables that consist of three or more categories, the weighted Kappa is frequently utilized. Weighted Kappa comes in two forms: linear weighted Kappa (LWK) and quadratic weighted Kappa (QWK).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides formulas for weighted Kappa and weights: w_ij^(m) = 1 - (|i-j|/(n-1))^m, where m≥1 (m=1 → LWK, m=2 → QWK). LWK attributes weights based on linear distance; QWK uses quadratic distance. Recommendation: report both LWK and QWK coefficients when not all disagreements carry equal weight to provide a more comprehensive understanding. Limitations: complexity and potential subjectivity in assigning weights; different weightings can produce varying results and require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match statistic to measurement scale and category count
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection between Cohen’s Kappa and weighted Kappa depends on whether the data are nominal (unordered) or ordinal (ordered) and on the number of categories (two vs three-or-more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: for ordered categorical variables with three categories (e.g., RECIST response categories PR, SD, PD) weighted Kappa is more appropriate than Cohen’s Kappa. Always choose the statistic that aligns with the variable type (nominal vs ordinal) and the substantive research question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify Kappa assumptions and study design fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa statistics (as used here) assume a fully-crossed design with precisely two raters and rater independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying Cohen’s or weighted Kappa, confirm that the study design meets these assumptions. If raters are not independent or the design is not fully crossed, using standard Kappa may be inappropriate and alternative reliability measures or adjusted analyses should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and report prevalence and bias effects (kappa paradox)
rubrics_metrics.description: One limitation of Cohen’s Kappa is its sensitivity to the prevalence of agreement in the data. High agreement but low Kappa ('kappa paradox') can occur when categories are imbalanced or when raters' marginal distributions differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate category prevalence and rater bias when interpreting Kappa. Cite classical discussions (e.g., Byrt et al.; Feinstein & Cicchetti) and consider supplementing Kappa with raw percent agreement or other diagnostics to explain paradoxical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation, interpretation, and transparent reporting of IRR statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should compute, interpret, and report IRR statistics (type of Kappa used, numeric values, and any inferential statistics) with enough detail to allow readers to understand and reproduce the assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which Kappa (Cohen/LWK/QWK) was computed, the formulas or software/method used, exact coefficient values, dataset (testing vs validation), p-values or confidence intervals where relevant, and any clarifications if reanalyses find discrepancies. The article demonstrates re-evaluating reported Kappa values and requests authors clarify mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider impact of IRR on downstream analyses and statistical power
rubrics_metrics.description: IRR affects the power of subsequent analyses for hypothesis testing; studies should address how the level of inter-rater agreement influences downstream statistical conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss and, if possible, quantify how measurement error due to imperfect IRR reduces effective sample size or power, and consider sensitivity analyses or adjustments when designing and analyzing studies that rely on rater-based outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative or equivalent reliability measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighted Kappa can be equivalent to the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) in some cases; other measures (e.g., percent agreement, ICC) may be appropriate depending on scale and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing IRR metrics, be aware of theoretical equivalences (Fleiss & Cohen) and practical differences. Use or report complementary measures when they help interpretation or when Kappa assumptions are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and justification of weighting scheme for weighted Kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of weights (linear vs quadratic or other schemes) for weighted Kappa relies on expert judgment or empirical evidence and affects the resulting coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which weighting scheme was used and justify it relative to the substantive meaning of category distances. Where appropriate, present results using more than one weighting (e.g., both LWK and QWK) to show sensitivity to weight choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret magnitude of kappa values contextually and cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels such as 'fair', 'moderate', or 'substantial' agreement depend on the chosen metric and can change with metric variant (Cohen vs LWK/QWK).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid reliance on generic cutoffs without context; illustrate with examples (the paper’s reanalysis changed qualitative labels when using weighted Kappa). Provide numeric values alongside qualitative descriptors and discuss clinical/research relevance of the observed agreement.
